intro: Large reviews link strong social ties and volunteering in later life with longer survival and better mood, and one randomized program shows gains in older adults' sense of purpose. Most of that evidence is observational, so it shows association more than proof.

items.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
items.finding: Across 148 studies (308,849 people), stronger social relationships were associated with a 50% greater likelihood of survival, comparable in size to some well-known risk factors.

items.title: Voluntary work for the physical and mental health of older volunteers: A systematic review
items.finding: The review found a positive effect of volunteering on mortality among people 65 and older and possibly on depression, with no evidence of harm, but effects were small and mostly from non-randomized studies.

items.title: The Baltimore Experience Corps Trial: Enhancing Generativity via Intergenerational Activity Engagement in Later Life
items.publisher: Journals of Gerontology Series B (via PubMed Central)
items.finding: In a randomized trial, older adults placed in school-based tutoring roles reported higher generative desire and achievement than controls, with larger gains for those who took part more.

items.title: Effect of Community Volunteering on Physical Activity: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.publisher: American Journal of Preventive Medicine (via PubMed Central)
items.finding: A randomized volunteer program increased walking activity among older women at higher risk of inactivity.

items.title: Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults: Opportunities for the Health Care System
items.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
items.finding: The consensus report describes social isolation and loneliness as serious public health risks, with about one quarter of community-dwelling Americans 65 and older considered socially isolated.

items.title: Loneliness and Social Isolation: Tips for Staying Connected
items.finding: The agency states that isolation and loneliness are associated with higher risks of depression, cognitive decline and other problems in older adults.

items.title: A Meta-Analysis of Interventions to Reduce Loneliness
items.publisher: Personality and Social Psychology Review (via PubMed Central)
items.finding: Single-group and non-randomized studies showed bigger effects than randomized ones, and among randomized studies the most successful interventions addressed maladaptive social thinking.

items.title: Intergenerational Programmes bringing together community dwelling non-familial older adults and children: A Systematic Review
items.publisher: Archives of Gerontology and Geriatrics (via PubMed Central)
items.finding: All 16 included studies reported positive effects, but the authors concluded there is neither strong evidence for nor against such programs because outcomes and methods varied and were unblinded.

items.title: Intergenerational programs: What can school-age children and older people expect from them? A systematic review
items.publisher: European Journal of Ageing (via PubMed Central)
items.finding: Of 11 studies reviewed, some showed gains in children's attitudes and older adults' health and quality of life, but the authors noted the benefits are not systematic.

limits: Most volunteering and social-tie findings are observational, so healthier people may simply volunteer more, and intergenerational program studies are small and uneven. The sheet's calls, apologies, storytelling and sitting with grief have little direct trial evidence, and nothing here is medical advice.
